newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Ringgit stays weak after touching 33-mth low.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ringgit stays weak after touching 33-mth low.

text.p: Malaysia's ringgit remained soft on Tuesday after hitting its weakest level in 33 months against the dollar, despite Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's supportive comments about the economy and currency, dealers and analysts said.
They said that although the ringgit recovered as funds took profits on the dollar, it remained vulnerable.

The ringgit touched 2.5700 per dollar overnight in New York, its weakest level since October 1994. But by 0600 GMT, the ringgit was trading around 2.5550/60 after closing at 2.5310/30 on Monday in Kuala Lumpur.
The Malaysian unit lost almost two percent against the dollar on Monday as speculators found a fresh target after attacking the Thai baht and Philippine peso.
Anwar said on Tuesday the ringgit was a victim of speculation and that it was not overvalued.
"My firm view is that under the prevailing economic and financial conditions, the ringgit is not overvalued," he told an Islamic capital market conference.
Anwar added that the Malaysian economy remained fundamentally sound due to policies long in place for balanced development and growth.
"Therefore, we are confident that once the speculative activity subsides, the trend for the ringgit will reverse to reflect the underlying favourable fundamentals," he said.

Anwar also stressed that while Malaysia was committed to ensure the ringgit would not fall prey to speculative activity, its policy of allowing market forces to determine the exchange rate remained unchanged.
"Given the speculative pressure on the ringgit, this is not surprising," said P.K. Basu, regional economist at UBS in Singapore.
"It's good not to be predictable. A flexible regime will make speculators think twice before hitting the ringgit," he said.

Dealers said the statement by Anwar reinforced their belief that the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, has swung its intervention strategy toward soothing intraday volatility, rather than vigorously defending a particular level.
Bank Negara sold dollars overnight through agents in New York at around 2.5700, dealers said. The central bank's presence was not detected this morning.
Dealers said the dollar/ringgit rate could reach 2.60 before it stablised, adding they expected trading to remain volatile in the short term.
"Speculators have won this battle, but not the war. Ultimately they will have to take profit. Then who will buy from them," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank.
Anwar said Malaysia did not favour a high interest rate regime in the long term.

"I don't think we are for (a) continued rise in interest rates, or a strong interest rate regime," he said, adding that the recent rise in interest rates was prompted by the recent speculative selling of the ringgit.

Analysts said that the rumoured injection of one-month funds by Bank Negara on Monday suggested that the central bank may be easing its defence of the ringgit in order to ensure that economic growth was not affected.
Bank Negara was believed to be lending funds to ease market liquidity and guide interest rates lower, market players said.
The benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) was fixed at 11.3 percent at 0300 GMT on Tuesday, down from 14.9 percent on Monday.
Interbank rates recently jumped to unusually high levels due to a sudden tightening of liquidity after massive intervention by the central bank in the foreign exchange market to defend the ringgit.
Although the actual size of the intervention was not known, dealers were estimating between $1 billion and $2 billion was drained from the system.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
